sentences.t:
Gewāt him ðā se hearda mid his hondscole
sylf æfter sande sǣwong tredan,
wīde waroðas.
sentences.l: Went for himself then the hard one with his hand-troop, himself along the sand to tread the sea-plain, the wide shores.
sentences.i: Then the stern hero himself went off with his band along the sand, treading the sea-plain, the broad shores.
sentences.n: The story resumes after the long aside on Hygd and on Offa’s queen that filled the last fitt. ‘Gewāt him … tredan’ is ‘went, for himself, … to tread’: ‘Gewāt’ is the past of ‘gewītan’, ‘go, depart’, ‘him’ a reflexive dative that only adds the sense of setting off on one’s own account, and ‘tredan’ an infinitive saying how he went. ‘se hearda’ is ‘the hard one’, Beowulf, an adjective used as a noun, with ‘sylf’ (‘himself’) beside it. ‘mid his hondscole’ is ‘with his hand-troop’: ‘scolu’ is a ‘troop’, and ‘hond-’ is most likely ‘picked, close at hand’ (his personal retinue), but that is a guess, as the compound is rare. ‘sǣwong’ is ‘sea-plain’ (‘sǣ’ ‘sea’, ‘wang’ ‘plain, field’), the beach; with ‘wīde waroðas’, ‘wide shores’ (an accusative plural of ‘waroð’), it is what he treads, while ‘æfter sande’ is ‘along the sand’.

sentences.t:
Woruldcandel scān,
sigel sūðan fūs.
sentences.l: The world-candle shone, the sun hastening from the south.
sentences.i: The sun, the candle of the world, shone, hastening from the south.
sentences.n: ‘Woruldcandel’ is ‘world-candle’, a kenning for the sun, and ‘sigel’ in the next half-line is a plain word for it: the same word also means ‘jewel, brooch’, but with ‘scān’ (‘shone’) it must be the sun here. ‘sūðan’ is ‘from the south’ and ‘fūs’ ‘eager, hastening’. I take the picture to be a sun standing in the southern sky, which is to say midday or after, but the exact sense of ‘fūs’ said of the sun is a guess.

sentences.t:
Hī sīð drugon,
elne geēodon, tō ðæs ðe eorla hlēo,
bonan Ongenþēoẹs burgum in innan,
geongne gūðcyning gōdne gefrūnon
hringas dǣlan.
sentences.l: They endured the journey, went with courage, until they learned of the shelter of earls, the slayer of Ongentheow, within the strongholds, the young war-king, the good, dealing rings.
sentences.i: They pressed on with their journey, boldly, until they learned that the protector of earls, the man who had slain Ongentheow, the good young war-king, was handing out rings in his stronghold.
sentences.n: ‘Hī sīð drugon’ is ‘they endured the journey’: ‘drugon’ is the plural past of ‘drēogan’, ‘carry out, endure’, and ‘elne geēodon’ ‘went with courage’, ‘elne’ a dative of manner. ‘tō ðæs ðe’ is ‘until’ (‘to the point that’). Everything after it is the object of ‘gefrūnon’, ‘they learned’ (past plural of ‘gefricgan’), and the objects are accusatives that all name one man, the king of the Geats: ‘eorla hlēo’ (‘shelter of earls’), ‘bonan Ongenþēoẹs’ (‘bonan’ is the accusative of ‘bona’, ‘slayer’) and ‘geongne gūðcyning gōdne’ (‘the young, good war-king’), with ‘hringas dǣlan’, ‘to deal rings’, an infinitive that goes with ‘gefrūnon’ as in ‘they learned of him dealing rings’. ‘burgum in innan’ is ‘within the strongholds’, a plural that probably stands for his one fortified hall. The king is Higelāc (named in the next unit). Ongentheow was the Swedish king, and the poem tells much later how he fell in the Geat-Swedish war; there Wulf wounds him first (2964–2966) and Eofor, ‘Higelāces þegn’ (2977; Eofor is named at 2964 and 2993), brings him down (2961–2981), so ‘bonan’ here credits the king with what his retainer did. The dot under the ‘ẹ’ in ‘Ongenþēoẹs’ is Klaeber’s sign that the vowel does not count in the metre: the name is scanned as if it were ‘Ongenþēos’. The same dot appears on the ‘ọ’ in ‘trūwọde’ at 1993.

sentences.t:
Higelāce wæs
sīð Bēowulfes snūde gecȳðed,
þæt ðǣr on worðig wīgendra hlēo,
lindgestealla lifigende cwōm,
heaðolāces hāl tō hofe gongan.
sentences.l: To Higelac was Beowulf’s journey quickly made known: that there, into the enclosure, the warriors’ shelter, the shield-companion, living, came, hale from battle-play, to the court to go.
sentences.i: Word was quickly brought to Higelac of Beowulf’s journey: that the shield-companion, the protector of warriors, had arrived in the courtyard alive and unhurt from the play of battle, and was walking to the hall.
sentences.n: ‘Higelāce wæs … gecȳðed’ is ‘to Higelac was … made known’: ‘gecȳðed’ is the past participle of ‘gecȳðan’, ‘make known’, ‘Higelāce’ the dative of the person told, ‘snūde’ ‘quickly’, and ‘sīð Bēowulfes’, ‘Beowulf’s journey’ (his return), the subject of the passive. The ‘þæt’ clause gives the news. In it ‘cwōm’ is ‘came’ and the infinitive ‘gongan’ says how he came, ‘came walking’. ‘on worðig’ is ‘into the enclosure’: ‘worðig’ is ‘enclosure, homestead, yard’, a rare word. ‘wīgendra hlēo’, ‘shelter of warriors’, uses the same word ‘hlēo’ that named Higelac in the last unit (‘eorla hlēo’), so Beowulf is given a king’s epithet. ‘lindgestealla’ is ‘shield-companion’ (literally ‘linden-companion’: ‘lind’ is the linden-wood shield, ‘gestealla’ a companion), and ‘heaðolāces hāl’ is ‘hale from battle-play’: ‘heaðolāc’ is a kenning for fighting (‘lāc’ ‘play, sport’), and ‘hāl’ ‘whole, unharmed’ is followed by a genitive saying in what respect.

sentences.t:
Hraðe wæs gerȳmed, swā se rīca bebēad,
fēðegestum flet innanweard.
sentences.l: Quickly was cleared, as the mighty one bade, for the foot-guests the hall-floor inward.
sentences.i: Room was quickly made, as the mighty king commanded, on the hall’s floor for the guests who had come on foot.
sentences.n: ‘Hraðe wæs gerȳmed’ is ‘quickly was cleared’, the past participle of ‘gerȳman’, ‘make room’, and its subject, ‘flet’, ‘floor, hall’, comes in the next line. ‘swā se rīca bebēad’ is ‘as the mighty one commanded’, ‘bebēad’ being the past of ‘bebēodan’, ‘command’, and ‘se rīca’ Higelac. ‘fēðegestum’ is a dative plural, ‘foot-guests’ (‘fēðe’ ‘going on foot’, ‘gest’ ‘guest’). The compound is found only here, and ‘guests who came on foot’, that is, who walked up from the shore, is a guess from its parts. ‘innanweard’ is ‘inward’, the inner part of the hall.

sentences.t:
Gesæt þā wið sylfne sē ðā sæcce genæs,
mǣg wið mǣge, syððan mandryhten
þurh hlēoðorcwyde holdne gegrētte,
mēaglum wordum.
sentences.l: Sat then beside the man himself he who had come through the strife, kinsman beside kinsman, after the lord-of-men through ceremonial speech the loyal one greeted, with weighty words.
sentences.i: Then the man who had come through the fighting sat down beside the king himself, kinsman by kinsman, when the lord of men had greeted his loyal follower in a formal speech, in solemn words.
sentences.n: ‘Gesæt … wið sylfne’ is ‘sat beside the very man’, ‘wið’ with the accusative ‘sylfne’, ‘himself’ (Higelac). ‘sē ðā sæcce genæs’ is ‘he who survived the strife’: ‘sē’ is the demonstrative used as ‘he who’, ‘genæs’ is the past of ‘genesan’, ‘come safe through’, and ‘ðā sæcce’ an accusative, the fights with Grendel and his mother. ‘mǣg wið mǣge’ is ‘kinsman beside kinsman’: Higelac is Beowulf’s uncle, since Beowulf’s mother was Hrethel’s daughter (374) and Higelac Hrethel’s son. ‘mandryhten’ is ‘lord of men’ (‘mann’ ‘man’, ‘dryhten’ ‘lord’), the subject of ‘gegrētte’, whose object is ‘holdne’, ‘the loyal one’, Beowulf. ‘syððan’ here gives the order of events, ‘after’, so the greeting was made before they sat. ‘þurh hlēoðorcwyde’ is ‘through speech-utterance’, ‘hlēoðor’ being ‘sound, voice’ and ‘cwide’ ‘saying’; I call it ‘ceremonial speech’, which is the sense the setting suggests rather than one the word proves. ‘mēaglum’ is a rare adjective, glossed ‘earnest, forceful’ in the lexica, and ‘weighty’ is a guess from them.

sentences.t:
Meoduscencum hwearf
geond þæt healręced Hæreðes dohtor,
lufode ðā lēode, līðwǣge bær
hæleðum tō handa.
sentences.l: With mead-cups went about through that hall-house Hæreth’s daughter; she loved the people, bore the drink-cup to the heroes’ hand.
sentences.i: Hæreth’s daughter went about that hall with the mead-cups; she was fond of the people, and carried the drinking-cup into the men’s hands.
sentences.n: ‘Hæreðes dohtor’ is Hygd, Higelac’s queen, named and praised at 1925–1931. ‘Meoduscencum hwearf’ is ‘with mead-cups went about’: ‘scenc’ is a serving-cup or pouring, ‘meoduscencum’ a dative plural, and ‘hwearf’ the past of ‘hweorfan’, ‘turn, go about’. ‘geond þæt healręced’ is ‘through that hall-house’ and the word is an emendation: Klaeber’s italic ‘heal’ replaces the manuscript’s ‘side’ (‘side ręced’, ‘wide house’), which is written over the line. Kemble (with a query), Thorkelin and three later editions also read ‘healreced’, Grein ‘hēa reced’ (‘high house’), and Holthausen thinks two half-lines have dropped out after ‘ręced’. (The ‘ę’ is Klaeber’s e caudata, an ‘e’ with a tail, which stands for ‘e’.) ‘lufode ðā lēode’ is ‘she loved the people’, ‘lēode’ an accusative plural. ‘līðwǣge’ is ‘drink-cup’ (‘līð’ ‘strong drink’, ‘wǣge’ ‘cup’), the object of ‘bær’. ‘hæleðum tō handa’ is ‘to the heroes’ hand’; the italic ‘le’ marks another change, for the manuscript has ‘hæ nū’ with a letter erased after the ‘æ’, and editors disagree: Grein and Sedgefield read ‘hælum’, Bugge, Schücking and Chambers ‘Hǣnum’ (= ‘Hǣðnum’), while Trautmann and Holthausen read ‘hæleðum’, as Klaeber does.

sentences.t:
Higelāc ongan
sīnne geseldan in sele þām hēan
fægre fricgcean, hyne fyrwet bræc,
hwylce Sǣ-Gēata sīðas wǣron:
sentences.l: Higelac began his hall-companion, in the hall, the high one, fairly to ask — curiosity broke him — what the Sea-Geats’ journeys were:
sentences.i: In that high hall Higelac began to put kind questions to his companion — his curiosity would give him no rest — about how the Geats’ journeys had gone:
sentences.n: ‘Higelāc ongan … fricgcean’ is ‘Higelac began to ask’, ‘ongan’ with the infinitive ‘fricgcean’, ‘ask, inquire’. ‘sīnne geseldan’ is ‘his hall-companion’, an accusative, from ‘geselda’, which the lexica give as ‘companion in the hall’ (‘sele’ ‘hall’). It is a rare word, and ‘his own’ is carried by ‘sīnne’. ‘in sele þām hēan’ is ‘in that high hall’, and ‘fægre’ ‘fairly, courteously’. ‘hyne fyrwet bræc’ is, word for word, ‘curiosity broke him’: ‘fyrwet’ is ‘curiosity’ and ‘bræc’ the past of ‘brecan’, with ‘hyne’ in the accusative; the nearest English is that it ‘pressed’ or ‘plagued’ him, which the idiomatic line puts as curiosity that gave him no rest. ‘hwylce … wǣron’ is an indirect question, ‘what the journeys were’, and ‘Sǣ-Gēata’ is the genitive plural of the people’s name (‘Sea-Geats’ in the literal line).

sentences.t:
‘Hū lomp ēow on lāde, lēofa Bīowulf,
þā ðū fǣringa feorr gehogodest
sæcce sēcean ofer sealt wæter,
hilde tō Hiorote?
sentences.l: ‘How did it befall you on the way, dear Beowulf, when you suddenly resolved far away to seek strife over the salt water, battle at Heorot?
sentences.i: ‘How did you fare on the way, dear Beowulf, when you so suddenly made up your mind to go far across the salt water to seek a fight, a battle at Heorot?
sentences.n: Higelac speaks, and the quotation mark opens. The spellings ‘Bīowulf’ and ‘Hiorote’ (earlier parts have ‘Bēowulf’, ‘Heorot’) belong to the second scribe of the manuscript, whose work Klaeber says begins at the end of 1939; ‘Ecgðīoes’ (1999) and ‘maðelode’ are probably the same hand’s spellings too, though Klaeber’s apparatus marks only where the second scribe begins. ‘hīo’ ‘she’ is not one of them, since it already stands at 1929 in the first scribe’s part. ‘Hū lomp ēow on lāde’ is ‘how did it befall you on the way’: ‘lomp’ is the past of ‘limpan’, ‘happen’, ‘ēow’ a plural dative, ‘you’ (Beowulf and his men, and he turns to the one man with ‘ðū’ in the next line), and ‘lād’ is ‘way, course, journey’. ‘þā ðū fǣringa feorr gehogodest’ is ‘when you suddenly, far, resolved’: ‘fǣringa’ ‘suddenly’, ‘gehogodest’ the second person past of ‘gehycgan’, ‘make up one’s mind’, and ‘feorr’ ‘far’. ‘sæcce sēcean’ is ‘to seek strife’, with its alliteration, and ‘hilde tō Hiorote’ repeats it as ‘battle at Heorot’, ‘hilde’ an accusative and ‘Hiorote’ the dative after ‘tō’.

sentences.t:
Ac ðū Hrōðgāre
wīdcūðne wēan wihte gebēttest,
mǣrum ðēodne?
sentences.l: But did you for Hrothgar the widely-known woe at all amend, for the famed lord?
sentences.i: And did you do anything to mend Hrothgar’s grief, known so far and wide, for that renowned king?
sentences.n: ‘Ac’ (‘but’; English would more naturally say ‘and’) opens a second question, and ‘gebēttest’ is the second person past of ‘gebētan’, ‘put right, make good’ (compare ‘bōt’, ‘remedy’). ‘wihte’ is a dative of ‘wiht’, ‘creature, thing’, used as an adverb, ‘in any way’. ‘Hrōðgāre’ and ‘mǣrum ðēodne’ are datives, ‘for Hrothgar, for the famed lord’, and ‘wēan’ is the accusative of ‘wēa’, ‘woe’. ‘wīdcūðne’ is ‘widely known’, agreeing with ‘wēan’, and it is an emendation: the manuscript has ‘wið’, Thorkelin read ‘wīd-’, and Klaeber’s italic ‘d’ shows the change. The account of Grendel’s twelve winters said the news of him spread in sad songs (149–151), which is why the woe could be ‘widely known’.

sentences.l: I for this with mind-care, with sorrow-surges, seethed; I trusted not in the journey of the dear man;
sentences.i: I seethed with anxiety over this, in surges of sorrow; I had no faith in the venture of a man so dear to me;
sentences.n: ‘Ic ðæs … sēað’ is ‘I for this seethed’: ‘ðæs’ is a genitive of cause, ‘on account of this’ (the journey), and ‘sēað’ the past of ‘sēoðan’, ‘boil, seethe’. ‘mōdceare’ (‘mind-care’) and ‘sorhwylmum’ (‘sorrow-surges’; ‘wylm’ is a welling, surge) are datives that say how. ‘sīðe ne trūwọde lēofes mannes’ is ‘I trusted not in the journey of the dear man’: ‘sīðe’ is a dative, ‘in the journey’, after ‘trūwian’, ‘trust’, and ‘lēofes mannes’ is a genitive that I take with it, ‘of the dear man’; the grammar would also allow the genitive to be the one trusted, ‘did not trust the dear man on the journey’. The dotted ‘ọ’ in ‘trūwọde’ is the sign explained at 1968.

sentences.t:
ic ðē lange bæd,
þæt ðū þone wælgǣst wihte ne grētte,
lēte Sūð-Dene sylfe geweorðan
gūðe wið Grendel.
sentences.l: I long begged you that you the slaughter-ghost not at all greet, let the South-Danes themselves have-it-out in war with Grendel.
sentences.i: I begged you long not to go near that slaughter-spirit, but to leave the South-Danes to settle their war with Grendel themselves.
sentences.n: ‘ic ðē lange bæd’ is ‘I begged you long’, ‘bæd’ the past of ‘biddan’, and the ‘þæt’ clause says what: ‘þæt ðū … ne grētte’, ‘that you not greet’, with ‘grētte’ a past subjunctive and ‘wihte’ ‘at all’. ‘grētan’ is ‘greet, address’ and also ‘approach, attack’, so ‘go near’ in the English. ‘wælgǣst’ is ‘slaughter-spirit’ (‘wæl’ ‘the slain’, ‘gǣst’ ‘spirit, ghost’), Grendel. ‘lēte … geweorðan’ is ‘let … come to be’ (in the literal line ‘have-it-out’ is my compression of the sense below), ‘lēte’ also a subjunctive, with the accusative ‘Sūð-Dene sylfe’, ‘the South-Danes themselves’, one of the compass-names for Hrothgar’s people, and ‘gūðe wið Grendel’ ‘in war with Grendel’. The sense of ‘geweorðan’ with ‘gūðe’ is a guess: the lexica give ‘be settled, be brought to an end’, and I take it as ‘let the South-Danes themselves get it settled in their war with Grendel’.

sentences.t:
Gode ic þanc secge,
þæs ðe ic ðē gesundne gesēon mōste.’
sentences.l: To God I say thanks for this, that I was allowed to see you safe.’
sentences.i: And I thank God that I have been allowed to see you safe and sound.’
sentences.n: ‘Gode ic þanc secge’ is ‘to God I say thanks’, ‘Gode’ a dative and ‘secge’ a present, ‘I say’. ‘þæs ðe’ is ‘for this, that’, a genitive of cause with ‘ðe’, so ‘because’. ‘mōste’ is the first-person past of ‘mōtan’, ‘be allowed’ (the form is the same in the indicative and the subjunctive), and ‘gesundne’ an accusative, ‘safe, sound’, agreeing with ‘ðē’. The closing quotation mark ends Higelac’s speech, which is anxious for the journey and relieved at the return.

sentences.t: Bīowulf maðelode, bearn Ecgðīoes:
sentences.l: Beowulf spoke in speech-words, child of Ecgtheow:
sentences.i: Beowulf spoke in formal words, the son of Ecgtheow:
sentences.n: The house rendering of the speech formula. ‘maðelode’ is the same word as ‘maþelode’ in the earlier parts (Klaeber prints it with either ‘þ’ or ‘ð’), the past of ‘maþelian’, which opens a formal speech. ‘Bīowulf’ and ‘Ecgðīoes’ are the second scribe’s spellings of ‘Bēowulf’ and ‘Ecgþēowes’, and ‘bearn’ is a nominative in apposition. The colon opens Beowulf’s report to Higelac, which runs past the end of this fitt.

sentences.t:
‘Þæt is undyrne, dryhten Higelāc,
(micel) gemēting, monegum fīra,
hwylc (orleg)hwīl uncer Grendles
wearð on ðām wange, þǣr hē worna fela
Sige-Scyldingum sorge gefremede,
yrmðe tō aldre;
sentences.l: ‘That is not-hidden, lord Higelac, (great) meeting, to many of men, what (strife)-while of us two, of Grendel, there was on that field, where he in many multitudes sorrow to the Victory-Scyldings brought about, misery for ever;
sentences.i: ‘It is no secret, lord Higelac, to many men — that great encounter — what a time of battle there was between Grendel and me on that field, where he brought sorrow in great numbers on the victorious Scyldings, misery without end;
sentences.n: The main clause is ‘Þæt is undyrne … monegum fīra’, ‘that is not hidden to many of men’, with ‘monegum’ a dative and ‘fīra’ a genitive plural, and ‘(micel) gemēting’, ‘(great) meeting’, in apposition to ‘Þæt’. The words in parentheses are restorations: the manuscript is defective here (apparatus), and ‘(micel)’ is a conjecture; Grein suggested ‘(mǣre)’, ‘famous’, and Moore ‘(mǣru)’. ‘gemēting’ is rare, ‘meeting, encounter’. ‘hwylc (orleg)hwīl’ is ‘what a time of strife’: Thorkelin supplied ‘(orleg-)’, ‘strife’, and ‘hwīl’ is ‘while, time’. ‘uncer Grendles’ is ‘of us two, of Grendel’s’: ‘uncer’ is the genitive dual, ‘of us two’ (Old English has a ‘we two’ form), and ‘Grendles’ stands beside it for the partner, ‘Grendel’s and mine’. ‘wearð’ is the past of ‘weorðan’, ‘come to be’. ‘on ðām wange’ is ‘on that field’; the fight was in the hall, so ‘wang’ is used loosely for the ground. ‘worna fela’ is literally ‘many of multitudes’, which I take as ‘in great numbers’ (‘worn’ ‘multitude’), an adverbial phrase beside ‘sorge’, which is singular, ‘sorrow’; and ‘Sige-Scyldingum’ (‘Victory-Scyldings’, the Danes, as at 597) is a dative. ‘yrmðe tō aldre’ is ‘misery for life’, so ‘for ever’, in apposition to ‘sorge’. The opening quotation mark begins Beowulf’s answer.

sentences.t:
ic ðæt eall gewræc,
swā begylpan [ne] þearf Grendeles māga
(ǣnig) ofer eorðan ūhthlem þone,
sē ðe lengest leofað lāðan cynnes,
f(ācne) bifongen. —
sentences.l: I avenged all that, so that [not] to boast of that dawn-clash needs any of Grendel’s kinsmen over earth, he who longest lives of the hateful race, enfolded in (crime). —
sentences.i: I avenged all of that, so that none of Grendel’s kin anywhere on earth need boast of that clash at dawn — not even the longest-lived of that hated stock, wrapped in crime. —
sentences.n: A tangle of damaged text. ‘ic ðæt eall gewræc’ is ‘I avenged all that’ (‘gewræc’ the past of ‘gewrecan’). In ‘swā begylpan [ne] þearf’ the word in brackets is added: the two 1787 transcripts have ‘swabe’ and ‘swal . .’, Kemble and others read ‘swā ne gylpan’, and Grein’s ‘swā begylpan [ne] þearf’, adopted by Klaeber, supplies the negative; without it ‘þearf’ (‘needs’) would say the opposite. ‘begylpan’ is ‘boast of’, taking the accusative ‘ūhthlem þone’, ‘that dawn-clash’; ‘ūht’ is the hour before daybreak, and ‘hlem’ is a rare word that I take as ‘crash, noise’, so ‘dawn-clash’ is a guess. ‘Grendeles māga’ is a genitive plural, ‘of Grendel’s kinsmen’, with ‘(ǣnig)’, ‘any’, restored from a transcript that shows ‘en . .’. ‘sē ðe lengest leofað lāðan cynnes’ is ‘he who lives longest of the hateful race’, in apposition to ‘ǣnig’. The last word, ‘f(ācne)’, is disputed: the transcripts give ‘fæ . .’ and ‘fer . .’, and editors have read ‘fǣr-’, ‘fenne’ (‘fen’) and ‘flǣsce’ (‘flesh’), while Bugge, Schücking, Sedgefield and Chambers read ‘fācne’, ‘in crime, in treachery’, and Klaeber follows them, citing Juliana 350 (the apparatus says only ‘so Jul. 350’). ‘bifongen’ is ‘enfolded, caught up’. The dash after the full stop is Klaeber’s, and begins a fresh start.

sentences.t:
Ic ðǣr furðum cwōm
tō ðām hringsele Hrōðgār grētan;
sentences.l: I there at first came to the ring-hall, Hrothgar to greet;
sentences.i: There, when I had only just come to the ring-hall to greet Hrothgar,
sentences.n: ‘Ic ðǣr furðum cwōm’ is ‘I there first came’: ‘furðum’ is a dative plural used as an adverb, ‘at first, just then’. ‘hringsele’ is ‘ring-hall’ (‘sele’ ‘hall’), the hall where rings are given out, that is, Heorot. ‘Hrōðgār grētan’ is ‘to greet Hrothgar’, ‘grētan’ an infinitive of purpose and ‘Hrōðgār’ its object. The sentence does not close here; its main verb is ‘getǣhte’ three lines on.

sentences.t:
sōna mē se mǣra mago Healfdenes,
syððan hē mōdsefan mīnne cūðe,
wið his sylfes sunu setl getǣhte.
sentences.l: straightway to me the famed son of Healfdene, after he my mind knew, beside his own sons a seat showed.
sentences.i: the famed son of Healfdene, as soon as he knew my purpose, assigned me a seat beside his own sons.
sentences.n: ‘se mǣra mago Healfdenes’ is ‘the famed son of Healfdene’, Hrothgar, with ‘sōna’ ‘at once’ and ‘mē’ a dative. ‘syððan hē mōdsefan mīnne cūðe’ is ‘after he knew my mind’: ‘cūðe’ is the past of ‘cunnan’, ‘know’, and ‘mōdsefan’ is ‘mind, heart, purpose’ (what Beowulf had come to do). ‘wið his sylfes sunu setl getǣhte’ is ‘showed a seat beside his own sons’, ‘getǣhte’ being the past of ‘getǣcan’, ‘show, assign’. ‘sunu’ could be a singular or a plural, and I read the plural: at 1188–1191 Beowulf sits beside Hrothgar’s two sons, Hrethric and Hrothmund.

sentences.t:
Weorod wæs on wynne; ne seah ic wīdan feorh
under heofones hwealf healsittendra
medudrēam māran.
sentences.l: The troop was in joy; I saw not in wide life, under heaven’s vault, of hall-sitters a greater mead-joy.
sentences.i: The company was in high delight; never in all my life, under the vault of heaven, have I seen a greater mead-revel among men sitting in hall.
sentences.n: ‘Weorod wæs on wynne’ is ‘the troop was in joy’. ‘ne seah ic wīdan feorh’ is ‘I did not see in wide life’: ‘wīdan feorh’ is an accusative of duration, ‘throughout a long life’, so ‘ever’, and ‘seah’ the past of ‘sēon’. ‘healsittendra’ is a genitive plural, ‘of hall-sitters’, depending on ‘medudrēam māran’, ‘a greater mead-joy’, where ‘drēam’ is ‘joy, revelry’ (not our ‘dream’). ‘heofones hwealf’ is ‘heaven’s vault’, the sky.

sentences.l: At times the famed queen, peace-kin of peoples, went through the whole floor, emboldened the young sons;
sentences.i: Now and then the famed queen, bond of peace between peoples, went all over the hall, heartening the young princes;
sentences.n: ‘mǣru cwēn’ is Wealhtheow, Hrothgar’s queen (612ff), who is not named here. ‘friðusibb folca’ is ‘peace-kin of peoples’, in apposition to the queen: ‘friðu’ is ‘peace’ and ‘sibb’ ‘kinship’. It belongs with the ‘peace-weaver’ (‘freoðuwebbe’, 1942), the woman whose marriage is meant to bind two peoples in peace, a role Freawaru is about to be given. ‘flet eall geondhwearf’ is ‘went through the whole floor’, ‘geondhwearf’ the past of ‘geondhweorfan’. ‘bælde byre geonge’ is ‘emboldened the young sons’: ‘byre’ is ‘sons’ (as at 1188, ‘hyre byre’, her sons). Klaeber’s italic ‘l’ shows an emendation, for the manuscript has ‘bædde’, and ‘bælde’, from ‘bældan’, ‘make bold’, is a proposal that Holthausen and Schücking took up; the sense ‘encouraged’ is what the emendation gives, and it is not certain.

sentences.t:
oft hīo bēahwriðan
secge (sealde), ǣr hīe tō setle gēong.
sentences.l: Often she a ring-band to a man (gave), before she to her seat went.
sentences.i: Often she would give a ring to some man before she went to her seat.
sentences.n: ‘oft hīo bēahwriðan secge (sealde)’ is ‘often she gave a ring-band to a man’. ‘sealde’ is restored in parentheses (the apparatus shows a new manuscript leaf, fol. 174b, beginning here with its first letters lost; Thorkelin supplied the word). ‘bēahwriða’ is ‘ring-band’ (‘bēag’ ‘ring’, ‘wriða’ ‘band’), an arm-ring or twisted ring, and ‘secge’ is the dative of ‘secg’, ‘man, warrior’. ‘ǣr hīe tō setle gēong’ is ‘before she went to her seat’: ‘hīe’ is the manuscript’s spelling (Grein and others prefer ‘hīo’), and since ‘gēong’ is singular, ‘hīe’ is ‘she’ here and not ‘they’.

sentences.t:
Hwīlum for (d)uguðe dohtor Hrōðgāres
eorlum on ende ealuwǣge bær,
þā ic Frēaware fletsittende
nemnan hȳrde, þǣr hīo (næ)gled sinc
hæleðum sealde.
sentences.l: At times before the (d)uguð, the proven troop, Hrothgar’s daughter to the earls at the end ale-cup bore, when I the hall-sitting ones Freawaru name heard, where she (nai)led treasure to the heroes gave.
sentences.i: At other times, before the veteran warriors, Hrothgar’s daughter carried the ale-cup to the earls at the far end of the hall, and then I heard those who sat in the hall name Freawaru, as she gave out the studded treasure to the men.
sentences.n: ‘dohtor Hrōðgāres’ is Hrothgar’s daughter, who is named two lines later as Freawaru. ‘for (d)uguðe’ is ‘before the retinue’, the veteran warriors, with the first letter restored (Grundtvig). ‘on ende’ is of uncertain sense: I take it as ‘at the end’ of the hall or bench, to the far end of the line of earls, but that is a guess, and Aant. queried ‘on handa’, ‘into the hand’ (as at 1983). ‘ealuwǣge bær’ is ‘bore the ale-cup’. ‘þā ic Frēaware … nemnan hȳrde’ is ‘when I heard … name Freawaru’, an accusative with an infinitive: ‘fletsittende’ (‘hall-sitters’) are the ones who do the naming, so Beowulf learned her name by hearing the men at the benches say it. ‘(næ)gled sinc’ is ‘nailed treasure’, ‘nægled’ being a participle of ‘næglan’, ‘stud with nails or rivets’ (Grein printed it as one word, ‘nægledsinc’), and I take it as treasure set with studs or gems, a guess; the letters ‘næ’ are restored, which the literal line shows as ‘(nai)led’. ‘hæleðum’ is a dative plural, ‘to the heroes’.

sentences.t:
Sīo gehāten (is),
geong goldhroden, gladum suna Frōdan;
sentences.l: She is promised, young, gold-adorned, to the glad son of Froda;
sentences.i: She is betrothed — young, adorned with gold — to the cheerful son of Froda;
sentences.n: ‘Sīo gehāten (is)’ is ‘she is promised’, ‘gehāten’ being the past participle of ‘gehātan’, ‘promise, betroth’; the ‘(is)’ is the restoration of Kluge and four editions, while Kemble and others read ‘(wæs)’, ‘was’. ‘geong goldhroden’ is ‘young, gold-adorned’, both nominatives, and ‘goldhroden’ the participle of ‘hrēodan’, ‘adorn’. ‘gladum suna Frōdan’ is ‘to the glad son of Froda’: ‘gladum’ and ‘suna’ are datives, ‘glad’ is ‘glad, bright, gracious’, and ‘Frōdan’ is the genitive of Froda. The bridegroom is not named in this passage. Beowulf later calls the bridegroom’s people the Heathobards (2032, 2037) and names Ingeld (2064). Hrothgar’s Danes and the Heathobards had a feud, and the match is the plan to end it that the next lines describe.

sentences.t:
(h)afað þæs geworden wine Scyldinga,
rīces hyrde, ond þæt rǣd talað,
þæt hē mid ðȳ wīfe wælfǣhða dǣl,
sæcca gesette.
sentences.l: (Has) of this decided the friend of the Scyldings, keeper of the realm, and counts it a counsel, that he by this woman a part of slaughter-feuds, of conflicts, would settle.
sentences.i: The friend of the Scyldings, keeper of the realm, has resolved on this, and thinks it a sound plan, that through this woman he may settle a part of their deadly feuds and quarrels.
sentences.n: ‘(h)afað þæs geworden’ is ‘has of this …’: the ‘h’ is restored (Kemble), ‘geworden’ is the past participle of ‘geweorðan’, and ‘þæs’ a genitive, ‘of this’. The lexica give ‘geweorðan’ the sense ‘agree, resolve’, so I read ‘has resolved on it’, and that is a guess at the idiom. ‘wine Scyldinga’ is Hrothgar (the ‘friend of the Scyldings’ of the earlier parts), and ‘rīces hyrde’ ‘keeper of the realm’. ‘ond þæt rǣd talað’ is ‘and counts that a counsel’, ‘rǣd’ ‘plan, good counsel’ and ‘talað’ the third-person present of ‘talian’, ‘reckon’. The ‘þæt’ clause gives the plan: ‘mid ðȳ wīfe’ is ‘by means of this woman’ (an instrumental), and ‘wælfǣhða dǣl, sæcca’ is ‘a part of slaughter-feuds, of conflicts’, two genitive plurals after ‘dǣl’, with ‘gesette’ a past subjunctive of ‘gesettan’, ‘settle, put down’.

sentences.t:
Oft seldan hwǣr
æfter lēodhryre lȳtle hwīle
bongār būgeð, þēah sēo brȳd duge!
sentences.l: Often, seldom anywhere, after a people’s-fall, for a little while the slayer-spear bows, though the bride be good!
sentences.i: Only rarely, anywhere, after a prince has fallen, does the deadly spear rest even a little while, however good the bride may be!
sentences.n: A famous crux, and the reading is disputed. ‘Oft seldan hwǣr’ puts ‘oft’ (‘often’) beside ‘seldan’ (‘seldom’), and Klaeber prints it as it stands. The apparatus lists the repairs: Kemble ‘Seldan ōhwǣr’, Heyne and others ‘Oft [nō] seldan’, Kluge ‘oft seldan (= sealdon) wǣre’, Holthausen ‘oft [bið] sēl and wǣr’, Sedgefield ‘oft sēlð onhwearf’. I print Klaeber’s text as it stands and read ‘rarely anywhere’, which the context seems to ask for; some of the repairs (Kluge, Holthausen, Sedgefield) change the sense, and the opening ‘Oft’ is unresolved. ‘lēodhryre’ is ‘fall of a people’s man’ or ‘fall of a people’ (‘lēod’ is both ‘man’ and ‘people’, ‘hryre’ ‘fall’), and in the English I take it as the fall of a prince. ‘lȳtle hwīle’ is ‘for a little while’, a dative or accusative of time (the form is the same), ‘for a little while’. ‘bongār’ is ‘slayer-spear’ (‘bona’ ‘slayer’, ‘gār’ ‘spear’), ‘būgeð’ the present of ‘būgan’, ‘bow, yield, sink’, so the spear rests. ‘þēah sēo brȳd duge’ is ‘though the bride be good’: ‘duge’ is a present subjunctive of ‘dugan’, ‘be of worth’. Beowulf is saying a bride seldom ends a blood-feud, however good she is.

sentences.t:
Mæg þæs þonne ofþyncan ðēodne Heaðo-Beardna
ond þegna gehwām þāra lēoda,
þonne hē mid fǣmnan on flett gæ̂ð, —
sentences.l: May it of this then displease the lord of the Heathobards and each of the thanes of those people, when he with the maiden into the hall goes, —
sentences.i: That may then vex the lord of the Heathobards, and every thane of that people, when he comes into the hall with the maiden —
sentences.n: ‘Mæg þæs … ofþyncan’ is ‘it may displease (on that account)’: ‘ofþyncan’ is an impersonal verb that takes a dative of the person, here ‘ðēodne Heaðo-Beardna’ (‘the lord of the Heathobards’; the passage does not say whether Froda or his son the bridegroom is meant) and ‘þegna gehwām’ (‘each of the thanes’), with ‘þæs’ the cause. ‘ðēodne’ is an emendation, marked by Klaeber’s italic ‘ne’: the manuscript has ‘ðeoden’, which would be a nominative and could not be the person vexed, and Kemble and others read the dative. ‘Heaðo-Beardna’ is the genitive plural of the people’s name, whose second part is ‘Beard’ (a tribal name); the 2037 form below is spelled differently. ‘þāra lēoda’ is ‘of those people’. ‘þonne hē mid fǣmnan on flett gæ̂ð’ is ‘when he goes with the maiden into the hall’ (the circumflex in ‘gæ̂ð’ is Klaeber’s contraction mark). Who ‘hē’ is, is settled by the clause after the dash. I take him as the young Dane of the next unit, one of the escort, so that the Heathobards are vexed to see a Dane walk their lord’s bride into the hall, although the grammar would also let ‘hē’ be the bridegroom. Klaeber’s dash begins an aside.

sentences.t: dryhtbearn Dena duguða biwenede;
sentences.l: a noble-child of the Danes, attended by the retinue;
sentences.i: a young Danish noble, attended by the retinue;
sentences.n: ‘dryhtbearn Dena’ is ‘noble-child of the Danes’, a young Danish nobleman (‘dryht’ ‘troop, company’, ‘bearn’ ‘child’; Kluge proposed ‘dryhtbeorn’, ‘noble warrior’), and he is the ‘hē’ of the line above. ‘duguða biwenede’ is a troubled phrase, and Klaeber prints the manuscript’s words. Thorkelin read ‘duguðe beþēnede’, ‘served by the retinue’, and Grein and others ‘duguða bī werede’, ‘defended by the retinue’. ‘biwenede’ is taken as a participle of ‘biwenian’, ‘attend on, entertain’, and ‘duguða’ is a genitive plural, ‘of the retainers’, so that taken strictly the sentence reads ‘entertained of the retainers’. I read ‘attended by the retinue’, the sense the proposals share, and the grammar of ‘duguða’ is a guess.

sentences.t:
on him gladiað gomelra lāfe,
heard ond hringmǣl Heaða-Bear[d]na gestrēon,
þenden hīe ðām wǣpnum wealdan mōston, —
sentences.l: on him gleam the old ones’ heirlooms, hard and ring-marked, the Heathobards’ treasure, while they those weapons to wield were permitted, —
sentences.i: on him gleam the heirlooms of their forefathers, hard and ring-patterned, the Heathobards’ treasure, for as long as they were allowed to wield those weapons —
sentences.n: The Heathobards are looking at the young Dane and at what he wears. ‘on him gladiað’ is ‘on him gleam’, ‘gladiað’ a plural present of ‘gladian’, ‘shine’ (from ‘glæd’, ‘bright’). ‘gomelra lāfe’ is ‘the old ones’ heirlooms’, ‘gomelra’ a genitive plural and ‘lāf’ ‘what is left’, so ‘inheritance’, with ‘heard ond hringmǣl’, ‘hard and ring-marked’, describing swords, whose blades probably carried ring patterns (compare ‘sceādenmǣl’). ‘Heaða-Bear[d]na gestrēon’ is ‘the Heathobards’ treasure’, the weapons being their own. The bracketed ‘d’ is added: the manuscript has ‘heaða bearna’, and ‘bearna’ would be ‘of the children’, so Thorkelin’s ‘Heaðo-beardna’ gives the sense wanted, and Klaeber keeps the manuscript’s ‘Heaða-’ with only the letter added. ‘þenden hīe ðām wǣpnum wealdan mōston’ is ‘while they might wield those weapons’: ‘hīe’ is the Heathobards, ‘wealdan’ takes the dative ‘wǣpnum’, and ‘mōston’ is a plural past, ‘were permitted’. The next fitt spells this out: an old Heathobard warrior says a Dane now wears a sword that the Heathobard youth’s father carried into his last fight, where the Danes killed him (2047–2056), so the fathers are dead and the Danes hold their weapons. The text ends on Klaeber’s dash in the middle of a sentence. It goes on in the next fitt, from line 2039, and this unit’s translation is left open on a dash for the same reason.
